Intermittent intravenous administration of nicotine activates neurohormonal pathways, leading to the release of acetylcholine, norepinephrine, dopamine, serotonin, vasopressin, beta-endorphin, growth hormone, and ACTH. 2. Nicotine nasal spray (Nicotine NS) is an aqueous solution of nicotine designed for administration as a metered spray to the nasal mucosa. 3. Nicotine is a tertiary amine composed of a pyridine ring and a pyrrolidine ring. 4. It is a colorless to pale yellow liquid that is freely water-soluble, strongly alkaline, oily, volatile, and hygroscopic, derived from the tobacco plant. 5. 6. Of its two stereoisomers, S(-)-nicotine is the more active form and is the predominant form found in tobacco and nicotine nasal spray. 7. The free alkaloid form of nicotine is rapidly absorbed through the skin, mucous membranes, and respiratory tract. 8. The chemical name of nicotine is S-3-(1-methyl-2-pyrrolidinyl)pyridine, with a molecular formula of C10H14N2 and a molecular weight of 162.23. 9. Nicotine has ionization constants of pKa1 = 7.84 and pKa2 = 3.04 at 15°C, and an octanol-water partition coefficient of 15:1 at pH 7. 10. Each 10 mL spray bottle of nicotine nasal spray contains 100 mg of nicotine (10 mg/mL) in an inactive vehicle with ingredients such as disodium phosphate, sodium dihydrogen phosphate, citric acid, methylparaben, propylparaben, edetate disodium, sodium chloride, polysorbate 80, aroma, and water. 11. The solution is isotonic with a pH of 7 and does not contain chlorofluorocarbons. 12. After priming the delivery system, each actuation of the nicotine nasal spray unit delivers a metered dose containing approximately 0.5 mg of nicotine. 13. The droplet size produced by the spray unit exceeds 8 microns, and one nicotine nasal spray unit delivers approximately 200 applications. 14. 15. Both acute and chronic tolerance to nicotine develop with smoking or ingestion of nicotine preparations. Acute tolerance, defined as a reduction in response to a given dose, develops rapidly (within less than 1 hour) but varies for different physiological effects such as skin temperature, heart rate, and subjective effects. 16. Withdrawal symptoms, including cigarette craving, can be alleviated in most individuals by plasma nicotine levels lower than those achieved through smoking. 17. Nicotine withdrawal in addicted individuals is characterized by symptoms such as craving, nervousness, restlessness, irritability, mood lability, anxiety, drowsiness, sleep disturbances, impaired concentration, increased appetite, minor somatic complaints (e.g., headache, myalgia, constipation, fatigue), and weight gain. 18. Nicotine toxicity manifests as nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, diaphoresis, flushing, dizziness, disturbed hearing and vision, confusion, weakness, palpitations, altered respiration, and hypotension. 19. Both smoking and nicotine increase circulating cortisol and catecholamines, and tolerance does not develop to the catecholamine-releasing effects of nicotine. 20. Changes in response to concomitantly administered adrenergic agonists or antagonists should be monitored when nicotine intake is altered during nicotine nasal spray therapy or smoking cessation. 21. Each actuation of nicotine nasal spray delivers a metered 50-microliter spray containing approximately 0.5 mg of nicotine. A single dose is defined as 1 mg of nicotine (two sprays, one in each nostril). 22. Following administration of two sprays of nicotine nasal spray, approximately 53% ± 16% (mean ± SD) enters systemic circulation. No significant differences in absorption rate or extent were observed due to deposition on different parts of the nasal mucosa. 23. Plasma nicotine concentrations from a single 1 mg dose of nicotine nasal spray rise rapidly, reaching maximum venous concentrations of 2–12 ng/mL within 4–15 minutes. The apparent absorption half-life is approximately 3 minutes. 24. There is wide intersubject variability in plasma nicotine concentrations from the spray. Approximately 20% of subjects reached peak nicotine concentrations similar to those seen after smoking one cigarette (7–17 ng/mL) following a 1 mg dose of the spray. 25. The volume of distribution following intravenous administration of nicotine is approximately 2 to 3 L/kg, and plasma protein binding of nicotine is less than 5%. 26. Changes in nicotine binding due to concomitant drug use or alterations in plasma proteins from disease states are not expected to significantly affect nicotine kinetics. 27. More than 20 metabolites of nicotine have been identified, all of which are less active than the parent compound. The primary urinary metabolites are cotinine (15% of the dose) and trans-3-hydroxycotinine (45% of the dose). 28. Cotinine has a half-life of 15 to 20 hours and concentrations that exceed nicotine by 10-fold. The liver is the major site of nicotine metabolism, with the kidney and lung also contributing. 29. About 10% of absorbed nicotine is excreted unchanged in the urine, which may increase to up to 30% with high urine flow rates and urinary acidification below pH 5. 30. The average plasma clearance of nicotine is approximately 1.2 L/min in a healthy adult smoker, and the apparent elimination half-life of nicotine from nicotine nasal spray is 1 to 2 hours. 31. The pharmacokinetics of nicotine nasal spray are well described by a two-compartment model with first-order input. Parameters derived from a 1 mg dose include an absorption rate constant (Ka) of 14.4 ± 7.3 hr⁻¹, an elimination rate constant (Ke) of 0.60 ± 0.53 hr⁻¹, distribution rate constants (K12 = 4.84 ± 2.57 hr⁻¹, K21 = 4.35 ± 2.30 hr⁻¹), and a volume of distribution over fraction absorbed (V/F) of 2.73 ± 0.82 L/kg in adults weighing 76 ± 15 kg. 32. No significant gender differences were observed in the pharmacokinetics of nicotine nasal spray, although intersubject variability (50% coefficient of variation) was noted for parameters such as AUC, Cmax, and clearance/kg. 33. The extent of nicotine absorption is slightly reduced (approximately 10%) in patients with the common cold or rhinitis. In these patients, peak plasma concentrations are reduced by approximately 20% (lower by 1.5 ng/mL on average), and the time to peak concentration is prolonged by approximately 30% (delayed by 7 minutes on average). 34. The use of a nasal vasoconstrictor such as xylometazoline in patients with rhinitis further prolongs the time to peak concentration by approximately 40% (delayed by 15 minutes on average), but the peak plasma concentration remains similar to those with rhinitis. 35. Nicotine itself does not appear to be a carcinogen in laboratory animals. However, nicotine and its metabolites increased tumor incidences in the cheek pouches of hamsters and the forestomach of F344 rats when combined with tumor initiators. 36. One study, which could not be replicated, suggested that cotinine, the primary metabolite of nicotine, may cause lymphoreticular sarcoma in the large intestine of rats. 37. Neither nicotine nor cotinine was mutagenic in the Ames Salmonella test, although nicotine induced repairable DNA damage.
